questions.knowledge_point: Estimating the Value of a Two-Variable Function
questions.problem:
Suppose that $f(x,y)$ is a differentiable function such that

$$
f(2,1)=2,\,{f}_{x}(2,1)=-1,\,{f}_{y}(2,1)=-1.
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,1),$ estimate the value of $f(1.98,0.94).$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(2,1)+∇f(2,1)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-1⟩ \\  & =f(2,1)+⟨{f}_{x}(2,1),{f}_{y}(2,1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,y-1⟩ \\  & =2+⟨-1,-1⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,y-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(1.98,0.94)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=1.98$ and $y=0.94,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.98,0.94) & ≈2+⟨-1,-1⟩\cdot ⟨1.98-2,0.94-1⟩ \\  & =2+⟨-1,-1⟩\cdot ⟨-0.02,-0.06⟩ \\  & =2+(-1)(-0.02)+(-1)(-0.06) \\  & =2+0.02+0.06 \\  & =2.08\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $f(x,y)$ be a differentiable function such that

$$
f(1,-1)=-2,\,{f}_{x}(x,y)=2xy-{y}^{2},\,{f}_{y}(x,y)={x}^{2}-2xy.
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,-1),$ estimate the value of $f(0.95,-1.04).$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,-1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(1,-1)+∇f(1,-1)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-(-1)⟩ \\  & ≈f(1,-1)+⟨{f}_{x}(1,-1),{f}_{y}(1,-1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y+1⟩ \\  & ≈-2+⟨{f}_{x}(1,-1),{f}_{y}(1,-1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y+1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{x}(1,-1)$ and ${f}_{y}(1,-1)$ using the given partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,-1) & =2(1)(-1)-(-1)^{2}=-3 \\ {f}_{y}(1,-1) & ={1}^{2}-2(1)(-1)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y)≈-2+⟨-3,3⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y+1⟩.
$$

Finally, we can estimate $f(0.95,-1.04)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=0.95$ and $y=-1.04,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0.95,-1.04) & ≈-2+⟨-3,3⟩\cdot ⟨0.95-1,-1.04+1⟩ \\  & =-2+⟨-3,3⟩\cdot ⟨-0.05,-0.04⟩ \\  & =-2-3(-0.05)+3(-0.04) \\  & =-2+0.15-0.12 \\  & =-1.97\end{aligned}
$$

f(0,1,-1)=-2,\,{f}_{x}(x,y,z)=z{e}^{x},\,{f}_{y}(x,y,z)=-1,\,{f}_{z}(x,y,z)={e}^{x}.

$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(0,1,-1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(0,1,-1)+∇f(0,1,-1)\cdot ⟨x-0,y-1,z-(-1)⟩ \\  & ≈-2+⟨{f}_{x}(0,1,-1),{f}_{y}(0,1,-1),{f}_{z}(0,1,-1)⟩\cdot ⟨x,y-1,z+1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,1,-1) & =(-1){e}^{0}=-1 \\ {f}_{y}(0,1,-1) & =-1 \\ {f}_{z}(0,1,-1) & ={e}^{0}=1\end{aligned}

Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y,z)≈-2+⟨-1,-1,1⟩\cdot ⟨x,y-1,z+1⟩.
$$

Finally, we can estimate $f(0.01,1.01,-0.99)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=0.01,y=1.01$ and $y=-0.99,$ as follows:

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Best Linear Approximation of a Multivariable Function
questions.problem: Let $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x+y).$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(0,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(0,1)+∇f(0,1)\cdot ⟨x,y-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(0,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =\frac{1}{1+x+y}\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{x}(0,1)=\frac{1}{2}, \\ {f}_{y} & =\frac{1}{1+x+y} &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{y}(0,1)=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(0,1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(0,1) & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(0,1)+∇f(0,1)\cdot ⟨x,y-1⟩ \\  & ≈\operatorname{ln}⁡2+⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\cdot ⟨x,y-1⟩ \\  & ≈\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\frac{x}{2}+\frac{y-1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=xy-\operatorname{ln}⁡z.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,1,e).$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,1,e)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,1,e)+∇f(1,1,e)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1,z-e⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(1,1,e)=0.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =y\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{x}(1,1,e)=1, \\ {f}_{y} & =x\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{y}(1,1,e)=1, \\ {f}_{z} & =-\frac{1}{z}\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{z}(1,1,e)=-\frac{1}{e}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(1,1,e)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(1,1,e) & =⟨1,1,-\frac{1}{e}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,1,e)+∇f(1,1,e)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1,z-e⟩ \\  & =0+⟨1,1,-\frac{1}{e}⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1,z-e⟩ \\  & =0+1(x-1)+1(y-1)-\frac{1}{e}(z-e) \\  & =-1+x+y-\frac{z}{e}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(2,8)+∇\,f(2,8)\cdot ⟨x-2,\,y-8⟩ \\  & =8+⟨2,\frac{1}{2}⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,\,y-8⟩ \\  & =8+2(x-2)+\frac{1}{2}(y-8) \\  & =2x+\frac{y}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Best Linear Approximation of a Multivariable Function
questions.problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=\frac{9}{x+2y-z}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,1,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,1,1)+∇f(2,1,1)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-1,z-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(2,1,1)=3.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =-\frac{9}{(x+2y-z)^{2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{x}(2,1,1)=-\frac{9}{(2+2(1)-1)^{2}}=-1, \\ {f}_{y} & =-\frac{18}{(x+2y-z)^{2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{y}(2,1,1)=-\frac{18}{(2+2(1)-1)^{2}}=-2, \\ {f}_{z} & =\frac{9}{(x+2y-z)^{2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{z}(2,1,1)=\frac{9}{(2+2(1)-1)^{2}}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(2,1,1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(2,1,1) & =⟨{f}_{x}(2,1,1),{f}_{y}(2,1,1),{f}_{z}(2,1,1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,-2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,1,1)+∇f(2,1,1)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-1,z-1⟩ \\  & =3+⟨-1,-2,1⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,y-1,z-1⟩ \\  & =3-1(x-2)-2(y-1)+1(z-1) \\  & =6-x-2y+z.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Best Linear Approximation of a Multivariable Function
questions.problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=xyz.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,-1,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,-1,-1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,-1,-1)+∇f(1,-1,-1)\cdot ⟨x-1,y+1,z+1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(1,-1,-1)=1.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =yz\,⇒\,{f}_{x}(1,-1,-1)=1, \\ {f}_{y} & =xz\,⇒\,{f}_{y}(1,-1,-1)=-1, \\ {f}_{z} & =xy\,⇒\,{f}_{z}(1,-1,-1)=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(1,-1,-1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(1,-1,-1) & =⟨{f}_{x}(1,-1,-1),{f}_{y}(1,-1,-1),{f}_{z}(1,-1,-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,-1,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,-1,-1)+∇f(1,-1,-1)\cdot ⟨x-1,y+1,z+1⟩ \\  & ≈1+⟨1,-1,-1⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y+1,z+1⟩ \\  & ≈1+(x-1)-(y+1)-(z+1) \\  & ≈-2+x-y-z.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Estimating the Value of a Two-Variable Function
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $f(x,y)$ be a differentiable function such that

$$
f(1,1) = 1, \quad f_x(x,y) = 2xy, \quad f_y(x,y) = x^2.
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,1),$ estimate the value of $f(1.1, 0.9).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y) \approx f(a,b) + \nabla f(a,b)\cdot \langle x-a, y-b \rangle.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(1,1)+∇f(1,1)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩ \\  & =f(1,1)+⟨{f}_{x}(1,1),{f}_{y}(1,1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩ \\  & =1+⟨{f}_{x}(1,1),{f}_{y}(1,1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find $f_x(1,1)$ and $f_y(1,1)$ using the given partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =2(1)(1)=2 \\ {f}_{y}(1,1) & =(1)^{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y) \approx 1 + \langle 2, 1 \rangle \cdot \langle x-1, y-1 \rangle.
$$

Finally, we can estimate $f(1.1, 0.9)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x= 1.1$ and $y=0.9,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.1,0.9) & ≈1+⟨2,1⟩\cdot ⟨1.1-1,0.9-1⟩ \\  & =1+⟨2,1⟩\cdot ⟨0.1,-0.1⟩ \\  & =1+0.2-0.1 \\  & =1.1\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Estimating the Value of a Three-Variable Function
canonical_examples.problem:
Suppose that $f(x,y, z)$ is a differentiable function such that

$$
f(1,2,5)=2, \quad  f_x(1,2,5)=4, \quad  f_y(1,2,5)=1, \quad f_z(1,2,5)=-2.
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,2,5)$ estimate the value of $f(1.01,2.02,4.95).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b, c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z) \approx f(a,b,c) + \nabla f(a,b,c)\cdot \langle x-a, y-b,z-c \rangle.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,2,5)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,2,5)+∇f(1,2,5)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-2,z-5⟩ \\  & =f(1,2,5)+⟨{f}_{x}(1,2,5),{f}_{y}(1,2,5),{f}_{z}(1,2,5)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-2,z-5⟩ \\  & =2+⟨4,1,-2⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-2,z-5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(1.01,2.02,4.95)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x= 1.01,$ $y=2.02,$ and $z=4.95$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.01,2.02,4.95) & ≈2+⟨4,1,-2⟩\cdot ⟨1.01-1,2.02-2,4.95-5⟩ \\  & =2+⟨4,1,-2⟩\cdot ⟨0.01,0.02,-0.05⟩ \\  & =2+0.04+0.02+0.1 \\  & =2.16\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Let $f(x,y, z)= xyz+y^2.$ Find the best linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(3, -1, 1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z) \approx f(a,b,c) + \nabla f(a,b,c)\cdot \langle x-a, y-b, z-c \rangle.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(3, -1, 1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(3,-1,1)+∇f(3,-1,1)\cdot ⟨x-3,y+1,z-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(3, -1, 1)= -2.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =yz\, &  & ⇒\, &  & {f}_{x}(3,-1,1)=-1, \\ {f}_{y} & =xz+2y\, &  & ⇒\, &  & {f}_{y}(3,-1,1)=1 \\ {f}_{z} & =xy\, &  & ⇒\, &  & {f}_{z}(3,-1,1)=-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(3, -1,1)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(3,-1,1) & =⟨-1,1,-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(3,-1,1)+∇f(3,-1,1)\cdot ⟨x-3,y+1,z-1⟩ \\  & =-2+⟨-1,1,-3⟩\cdot ⟨x-3,y+1,z-1⟩ \\  & =-2-(x-3)+(y+1)-3(z-1) \\  & =-2-x+3+y+1-3z+3 \\  & =5-x+y-3z.\end{aligned}
$$
